query: For high-entropy-alloy multilayer protective coatings, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation? Specify what governs the behavior and why, an unspecified controlled comparison that would reveal it, the expected observations relative to a baseline, applicable boundaries, supporting evidence, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In high-entropy-aloy multilayer protective coatings, the alternating layers create internal interfacial barriers that impede dislocation motion (both glide and climb), thereby reducing time-dependent plastic (creep) deformation compared to homogeneous single-phase coatings.
generation.material_initial_state: Multilayer high-entropy alloy protective coatings composed of alternating layers of closely related HEA compositions (e.g., alloys similar to AlCoCrFeNi or AlxCr0.2NbTiV), each layer having slightly different lattice parameters and phase characteristics.
generation.intervention: Fabricate two sets of coatings: one with a multilayer architecture (alternating layers with intentionally designed lattice mismatch or phase variations) and a control set with a homogeneous single-phase high-entropy alloy composition.
generation.conditions: Subject both sample sets to sustained high-temperature conditions (e.g., near 1000 °C) under constant mechanical load sufficient to induce creep behavior over extended periods.
generation.structural_mediator: The interfaces between the individual layers generate localized misfit strains and act as obstacles that limit dislocation motion, suppressing the accumulation and climb of dislocations during high-temperature loading.
generation.mechanism: The layered structure disrupts the continuous paths required for dislocation glide and climb by producing periodic barriers. These interfaces, due to lattice mismatch and possible phase transformation discrepancies, result in dislocation pile-ups, reducing the effective creep strain rate compared to a uniform microstructure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature stress, the multilayer coating will exhibit a significantly lower creep rate (reduced time-dependent plastic deformation) than the homogeneous control sample. Observable differences include reduced strain accumulation over time and possibly higher strain-rate sensitivity due to interfacial hindrance.
generation.baseline: Homogeneous high-entropy alloy coating of similar overall composition but lacking the deliberately introduced multilayer architecture.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to be effective within high operational temperatures where dislocation-mediated creep dominates (near 1000 °C) and when the layer thickness and lattice mismatch are sufficient to act as barriers; extreme conditions leading to complete diffusion or loss of interfacial integrity may diminish the effect.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of creep reduction and the optimal layer thickness/misfit conditions remain to be determined experimentally. The influence of competing high-temperature oxidation processes on the interfacial integrity also requires further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples as described – multilayer and homogeneous high-entropy alloy coatings. Subject both sets to a constant load creep test at a high temperature (e.g., 1000 °C) for an extended period. Use identical substrate and environmental conditions to isolate the effect of the multilayer architecture.
measurements: Measure the strain evolution over time via high-resolution dilatometry or in-situ imaging techniques.
Characterize the dislocation density and distribution near interfaces post-test using TEM or EBSD.
Evaluate any phase transitions or changes in layer integrity through X-ray diffraction or SEM imaging.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the multilayer coatings do not show a statistically significant reduction in creep rate (or if the dislocation density profiles do not indicate effective interfacial blockage) compared to the homogeneous control, then the hypothesis that interfacial barriers are the dominant mechanism for creep reduction is falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractAs protective coatings for the thermal parts of aero-engines, AlCoCrFeNi coatings have good application prospects. In this study, atmospheric plasma spraying (APS) was used to prepare AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy coatings (HECs), which were oxidized from 650 °C to 1000 °C. The mechanism of the oxide layer formation and the internal phase transition were systematically investigated. The results show that a mixed oxide scale with a laminated structure was formed at the initial stage of oxidation. The redistribution of elements and phase transition occurred in the HECs’ matrix; the BCC/B2 structure transformed to Al-Ni ordered B2 phase and Fe-Cr disordered A2 phase.Keywords: plasma spraying, oxidation behavior, high-entropy coatings, phase transition

AbstractHigh-temperature creep refers to the slow and continuous plastic deformation of materials under the effects of high temperatures and mechanical stress over extended periods, which can lead to the degradation or even failure of the components’ functionality. AlxCr0.2NbTiV (x = 0.2, 0.5, or 0.8) refractory high-entropy alloys were fabricated by arc melting. The effects of Al content on the microstructure of AlxCr0.2NbTiV alloys were studied using X-ray diffraction, scanning electron microscopy, and electron backscatter diffraction. The microhardness, compression properties, and nanoindentation creep properties of AlxCr0.2NbTiV alloys were also tested. The results show that the AlxCr0.2NbTiV series exhibits a BCC single-phase structure. As the Al content increases, the lattice constant of the alloys gradually decreases, and the intensity of the (110) crystal plane diffraction peak increases.
